synopsis: NIOSH’s 2022 rapid review covered 64 articles from 2000–2020 and 97 haul-truck collision-system cases; evidence largely concerned components or prototypes, only 8% of articles exceeded technology readiness level 7, and only 10% of cases involved avoidance or intervention systems [f5933, f393, f5172, f5171]. The strongest cited hard false-alarm evidence remains the 2006 Caterpillar 793B radar study: among 580 alarms over 618 reversals, 102 (18%) were false and 243 (42%) were nuisance alarms, while the audible alarm was found switched off after shifts [f102, f5174, f5175, f104]. Historical NIOSH evidence counted 22 blind-area fatalities from 2000 to mid-2006, with 67% of victims behind reversing equipment, but these data must not be treated as a 2026 fatality rate [f3060, f11546, f3068]. Research emphasis on vehicle-to-vehicle interactions does not match accident coverage: a later analysis of 54 fatality reports identified 21 berm-related and 12 dump-point-related deaths, versus 13 involving pedestrians or vehicles [f395, f3070, f3072]. Practical findings show that radar placement matters, stopping can fail when downhill grade exceeds brake capacity, and underground stop zones varied across sites by an average 1.4 m and up to 3.6 m [f7039, f7040, f5903, f5929]. Planning still faces gaps in false-positive testing, simulation procedures, environmental effects and real-world validation, alongside mostly undisclosed manufacturer validation documentation and the warning that new technology can introduce new hazards [f10425, f10448, f1370].
